title: The Instrument Named After the Word for Quiet
blurb: The piano is named for the one thing a harpsichord could never do: play soft. Inside sit 230 steel strings and a hammer that lets go.

blocks.prompt: What Is Hiding Inside a Piano
blocks.text: A piano looks simple on the outside. It is just a long row of black and white keys. Inside, it is busy. When you press a key, a small wooden hammer swings up and taps a string. The string shakes very fast, and that shaking is the sound you hear. Let the key go and a soft pad drops onto the string to stop the sound. Press gently and you get a quiet note. Press hard and the hammer swings faster, so the note is loud. A piano has 88 keys. The fat strings on the left make low notes. The short thin strings on the right make high notes.

blocks.prompt: The Keyboard That Could Not Whisper
blocks.text: Three hundred years ago, the fanciest keyboard instrument was the harpsichord. It was beautiful, and it had one big problem. Inside a harpsichord, pressing a key made a tiny quill pluck a string. A pluck is a pluck. It sounds the same whether you press the key gently or bang it. A harpsichord player could not play loud and soft. An Italian instrument maker named Bartolomeo Cristofori decided to fix that. Around the year 1700, in Florence, he built a keyboard with hammers instead of quills. Press the key gently and the hammer taps the string gently. Press hard and the hammer flies up fast and the note rings out loud. For the first time, a keyboard could get louder and softer under the player's fingers. Cristofori called his invention a harpsichord with soft and loud. In Italian, soft is piano and loud is forte. People shortened the long name to pianoforte, then shortened it again. Today we just say piano. So the instrument that finally learned to play loud ended up named after the word for soft.

piano means soft and forte means loud

blocks.prompt: The Machine Under the Lid
blocks.text: From the outside, a piano is a piece of furniture. Open the lid and you find a machine. A grand piano holds roughly 230 steel strings, stretched so tightly that together they pull with a force of about twenty tons. Nothing made of wood could survive that, so the strings are anchored to a heavy plate of cast iron. Pressing a key sets off a chain of small wooden parts called the action. The important trick happens at the very end. Just before the hammer reaches the string, it lets go of the machinery and flies the last short distance on its own. Piano makers call this the escapement. It matters because a hammer still connected to your finger would rest against the string and smother the note the instant it was born. Instead the hammer strikes, bounces away, and the string is left ringing. The string on its own is far too thin to move much air, so its vibration passes down through a wooden bridge into the soundboard, a wide sheet of spruce that fills the body of the piano. The soundboard shakes the air in the room. That is what you actually hear. When you lift your finger, a felt damper drops back onto the string and the note stops. Hold down the right pedal and every damper lifts at once, so the whole instrument is left open and ringing.

blocks.prompt: The Invention Nobody Wanted
blocks.text: Bartolomeo Cristofori spent his life as the keeper of instruments for the Medici family in Florence, and around 1700 he built something that had never existed: a keyboard whose hammers could strike a string hard or soft depending on the player's touch. It should have made him famous immediately. It did not. Almost nobody bought one. The instrument was expensive, its sound was thin next to a harpsichord, and musicians had spent two centuries learning to make music without needing loud and quiet in the first place. Three of Cristofori's pianos survive today, in New York, Rome, and Leipzig. What saved the idea was a magazine article. In 1711 an Italian writer named Scipione Maffei published a description of Cristofori's invention, complete with a diagram of the action. The article was translated into German, and German builders started copying the drawing. Gottfried Silbermann built pianos from it. When Johann Sebastian Bach tried an early Silbermann, he complained that the high notes were weak and the keys too heavy to play. Silbermann took the criticism badly, went away, and improved the design. Years later Bach played the newer version and approved it. The piano then spent a century getting stronger. Builders wanted more volume for bigger concert halls, which meant thicker strings under greater tension, which meant frames that kept breaking. The answer arrived in Boston in 1825, when Alpheus Babcock cast a piano frame in a single piece of iron. Around the same time a Paris maker, Henri Pape, replaced leather hammer coverings with felt, which gave the instrument a warmer, rounder tone. By the 1880s the keyboard had settled at 88 keys, the range it still has today. The result is the instrument Cristofori was reaching for and never heard: loud enough to fill a hall, quiet enough to whisper, and able to do both inside the same phrase.

notes: Equal temperament: 12 equal steps per octave
Almost no interval on a piano is pure
Inharmonicity: stiff strings ring slightly sharp

The Railsback curve, measured in 1938
Lowest note 27.5 Hz, highest 4186 Hz

blocks.prompt: The Piano Is Out of Tune, and That Is on Purpose
blocks.text: Here is a strange fact about the instrument in the corner of the living room: a well tuned piano is not in tune. It cannot be. The piano is a machine built on compromises, and every one of them was chosen deliberately. Start with the first compromise. When two notes sound good together, it is because the numbers behind them are simple. Play a note, then play a note whose string vibrates exactly twice as fast, and your ear hears the same note higher up: an octave. A ratio of three to two gives a fifth, the most solid interval in music after the octave. For centuries, keyboards were tuned to make these simple ratios exact, and the results were gorgeous in a few keys and unbearable in the rest. Stack pure fifths on top of each other and they never land back where they started. The mathematics simply does not close. Somewhere in the circle, one interval has to absorb all the leftover error, and that interval howls so badly that tuners named it the wolf. The fix was to spread the error out. Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve steps of exactly the same size, which means almost no interval on the piano is pure. The fifths are all a hair narrow. The major thirds are noticeably wide. Nothing is perfect, but nothing is a wolf either, and a piece can wander through every key without falling off a cliff. Every chord you have ever heard on a piano is slightly wrong on purpose. Then comes the second compromise, and this one is physics, not choice. The neat rule that a string's overtones are exact multiples of its main pitch is only true of an ideal string: perfectly flexible, infinitely thin, existing only in a textbook. Real piano strings are made of stiff steel wire. Stiffness fights bending, and the higher overtones bend the string more sharply, so they ring slightly sharper than the math predicts. Physicists call this inharmonicity, and every piano has it. Short, thick strings have more of it, which is why small uprights suffer more than long concert grands. Inharmonicity means a tuner cannot tune a piano to a chart. If the top octave were set to mathematically correct frequencies, it would sound flat against the overtones already ringing out of the strings below it. So tuners stretch the tuning: the treble is pulled slightly sharp, the bass slightly flat, each note tuned not to a number but to the sound of the instrument itself. In 1938 an American physicist, O. L. Railsback, measured how real tuners actually worked and found this stretch curve hiding in nearly every piano he tested. Nobody had told them to do it. They were tuning by ear, and their ears had been quietly obeying the physics all along. So the piano is a stack of accepted errors: a scale that is evenly wrong so that no key is unusable, and an octave that is deliberately widened so that a stiff steel wire sounds right to a human being. It is a compromise built out of compromises. It is also the instrument almost everyone learns music on, which suggests the compromises were the correct ones.
